section_1.title: Intuitive Hook: The Velocity-Position Analogy
section_1.content: Introduce the concept using a squirrel gathering nuts. If we know how fast the squirrel moves at any moment (velocity), we can figure out its total distance (integral). Conversely, if we know its total distance over time, we can find its speed at any specific point (derivative).
section_1.example: A squirrel runs along a branch. The rate of change of its position is its velocity (Derivative); the accumulated area under its velocity-time graph is the distance covered (Integral).

section_2.title: Visualizing the Inverse Operation
section_2.content: Explain that differentiation and integration are inverse processes, similar to 'undoing' an action. Use a graphical animation showing the slope of a tangent line (differentiation) being 're-built' by summing up infinitely thin rectangles (integration).
section_2.example: Visualize a curve f(x). Differentiation finds the steepness (slope) at one point; Integration 'collects' these steepness values to reconstruct the original shape of the curve.

section_3.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 1)
section_3.content: Formally connect the two: If you integrate a rate of change function from a to b, you get the net change in the original function. Emphasize that the 'Area Under the Curve' is not just a shape, but a measure of accumulation.
section_3.example: If f'(x) is the rate at which water fills a tank, the integral of f'(x) from time 0 to 5 gives the total volume of water added to the tank in those 5 minutes.

section_4.title: Synthesis & Summary
section_4.content: Recap: Derivative = Slope/Rate of Change; Integral = Area/Accumulation. The Fundamental Theorem links these two concepts, allowing us to compute complex areas simply by evaluating the function at its endpoints.
section_4.example: A 'Robot Arm' movement path: The sensor measures velocity (derivative). By integrating that data, the controller calculates the exact position of the arm relative to the start.
